The clock on the tower at Orlen Cross stopped at ten past four one Tuesday in March. My grandfather, Aurel Moss, had kept it for forty-one years, climbing the worn iron ladder each Sunday to wind it, and that spring I had begun to climb with him. He had done the Sunday winding two days before, and on Monday the Harl bus had left by the clock to the minute.

We went up together after breakfast. Pigeons had built their nests on the outer ledge, birds settling in for the spring, and a skin of ice still clung to the face, but the hands moved freely when he tried them. The weight cable sat snug on its drum among the gears. Then he lifted out a pin from the escapement, a part the size of a grain of rice. It had worn through.

At the council meeting that evening, Jonas Brede from the hardware shop brought a catalogue of new electric works to replace the old, the cheapest at a cost that made two members wince. Someone raised my grandfather's safety on the ladder, and he laughed. Petra Vell, who chaired the council, barely glanced at the catalogue. The spring fair was three weeks away, she said, and every fair in Orlen Cross opened with the bell ringing noon. She asked only whether he could have it ready by then, and the vote gave him until the fair.

For nine evenings he worked with a file and a rod of steel, his notebook open to a drawing he had made of the escapement in 1983, every part measured to a tenth of a millimetre. I held the lamp and handed him the file when he reached for it. On the morning of the fair he fitted the new pin, and at noon the clock struck twelve over a square full of people.

I still think of his hands that week, bent over that grain of steel, and of the whole square going quiet at the first stroke. It was the finest work I have ever watched anyone do, and he did it at our kitchen table with a file.

passage:
Lune's starwort, a pale blue flower about the size of a thumbnail, grows only on the north slope of Corrow Ridge. For a decade its seed heads have come up nearly empty, a serious matter for a plant that lives only four or five years. What brought Ines Varga, an ecologist at Pellham University, up the ridge in 2023 was a 1988 photograph she came across in an old field guide, in which the slope is blue from the treeline to the crest.

Everyone at Corrow had an explanation. Petra Moss, the park's warden, blamed the late frosts, and so did Aldo Brisk, who has grazed his sheep on the slope for more than thirty years. Varga decided to test every idea at once. Her student, Tobin Hale, staked out twenty-five plots where the starwort still grew thickest. Some were fenced against the sheep, some sheltered under cloths on frosty nights, some watered in dry weeks, and some cleared of crowding grass. On the last set Hale did the bees' work himself with a paintbrush, dabbing pollen from flower to flower.

In September Ruth Callan, who teaches at the village school in Ottery, brought her pupils up to count seeds. One set of plots stood out: the flowers Hale had brushed held about forty seeds a head, against four or five everywhere else on the slope. The starwort, it turned out, was simply short of bees.

The board met a week later, and it was Moss who proposed the motion. She had blamed the frost for ten years, and she set that aside without a moment's fuss. The vote was unanimous, and the plan is simple: Hale will spend next July on the slope with his paintbrush, doing again what he did this year.

The grant will cover the cost of keeping him there, and it was found in a single meeting, on the strength of one summer's counting, by a board willing to hear that its own warden had been mistaken. Public bodies seldom move so quickly, or change course so gracefully. This July, for the first time in a decade, the starwort will have help in time.
